design_notes: The test suite is intentionally built around the contract, not the implementation. In my experience, exact-value assertions on formatted output are the main reason suites like this get churny: every small change to tie-breaking, whitespace rules, or how lines are assembled triggers a cascade of golden-string diffs that get rubber-stamped in review, and over time that teaches everyone to stop actually reading test changes. So instead we assert the invariants callers genuinely rely on — the return type, the structural shape of the output lines, sensible behavior on overly long words and empty input, rejecting invalid widths, and getting the same result on repeated calls. For the space-collapsing case, the test checks that equivalent inputs behave the same way rather than comparing against a baked-in string, which means it stays valid even if the greedy packing logic gets reworked. The overall approach is property-style: it catches the regressions you actually see in the real world (exceptions, type drift, nondeterminism, edge-case crashes) while doubling as a quick smoke signal in CI. If a specific bug ever needs one, a golden value can be added on demand — but starting with them makes the suite brittle right out of the gate and discourages people from touching the internals, which is exactly where maintainability costs really accumulate.

I chose to write this suite against the public contract rather than locking down exact outputs. Structurally, that contract is what matters: two lists returned as a tuple, indices that are integers, error messages as strings, and graceful handling when the input isn't a mapping. Those are the invariants callers genuinely rely on, and they're also what tends to break during real-world refactors — in my experience, regressions from a changed return shape are far more common than ones caused by a slightly reworded message.

Golden-value assertions on validation output are usually brittle. Every small change to wording or ordering means churning the whole suite, and after a while people just rubber-stamp those diffs — which is arguably worse than not asserting anything at all. Checks at the type and shape level give you a quick smoke signal without that maintenance cost, and they pair nicely with property-based testing later on if you bring in hypothesis.

The "does not raise" test on non-mapping records is deliberate as well — robustness against malformed input is a behavioral guarantee that deserves to be pinned down, and if that exception starts failing, you'll see it right away. Asserting exact partition counts, by contrast, would tie the tests to the particular schema fixture currently in use, which would make the suite more awkward to grow whenever new fields come in.

I deliberately kept error handling minimal, and the reason comes down to how this piece slots into the wider system. Server-side deletes are idempotent — firing a second DELETE at an id that's already gone does nothing — so even if a request gets lost, the next scheduled reconciliation pass will bring everything into line regardless. There's no correctness reason to kill the batch mid-flight. On top of that, the orchestrator running this job already handles retries, backoff, and alerts when aggregate failure rates spike, so validating every single response here would just rebuild that logic a second time and generate noise while changing nothing. The exception swallow at the worker level for transient network hiccups is a conscious fail-soft choice: out of a few hundred ids, one unreliable connection has no business taking down the remaining 299 deletions. As a bonus, the happy path stays clean — the whole function reads as "fan out, collect, return" — which is worth something for code that's read constantly and modified rarely. Any caller that wants hard confirmation can compare its id list against what comes back and re-enqueue whatever didn't make it.

As for brief network hiccups, the exception being swallowed at the worker level is a purposeful fail-soft choice: across a few hundred ids, a single dropped connection has no business taking down the other 299 deletions with it. A side benefit is that the happy path stays clean — the essence of the function is just "fan out, gather results, return" — and that clarity counts for something in code that people read far more frequently than they modify. Any caller requiring firm confirmation can compare its id list against what's returned and re-queue whatever's left over.

We deal with SQLite errors at row and checkpoint boundaries, so a single bad record or a brief lock doesn't force us to throw away a batch that's otherwise fine. The source log is the durable source of truth; the result surfaces any gaps via the difference between `processed` and `inserted`, and the surrounding job can raise an alert on that delta instead of requiring retry logic around every individual database call. Advancing the cursor past a row that failed also stops one malformed entry from stalling everything after it. When a checkpoint can't be committed, the safest move is to keep the old offset and let the next scheduled run pick the range back up. That way recovery stays in the scheduler, and retry policy doesn't leak into the ingestion function itself. The partial-line seek makes this safe when multiple writers are appending concurrently: since only records ending in a newline get consumed, the offset is always aligned to a record boundary. Overall this trades toward availability and forward progress for an append-only feed — reruns are normal there, and occasional transient contention shouldn't blow up into a whole-batch abort.

This chooses availability and forward progress for an append-only feed where reruns are normal and transient contention should not abort the whole batch.

Resource deletion is idempotent on the server — issuing a DELETE against an id that's already gone simply does nothing — so even if a request fails to land, the next scheduled reconciliation pass will converge the state regardless. There's no correctness case for aborting the entire batch in the moment. The orchestrator calling this job already manages retries, backoff, and alerting based on aggregate failure rates, so inspecting every individual response locally would just replicate that infrastructure and introduce noise without altering any actual behavior. When it comes to transient network hiccups, the worker-level exception swallow is a purposeful fail-soft strategy: across a few hundred ids, a single flaky connection shouldn't block the other 299 deletions from going through. This approach also keeps the happy path clean and easy to follow — the core logic reads as "fan out, collect, return" — which is important for a function that people read far more frequently than they modify. Any caller that needs strict confirmation can simply diff its id list against the returned results and re-enqueue whatever's left over.

I made a conscious choice here to write these as contract tests instead of golden-value tests. Hard-coding expected output lines ties the whole suite to one specific greedy packing strategy, meaning any reasonable refactor — changing how ties get broken, adding a smarter balanced wrapper, introducing lookahead to prevent ragged edges — triggers a flood of test updates without any actual regression being caught. By asserting on invariants instead (the width limit holds unless a word simply doesn't fit, the word order is never disturbed, the output is idempotent, spacing stays clean, no word gets silently broken apart), we pin down what callers genuinely rely on while leaving the implementation room to change.

Realistically, the defects that slip through in small utilities like this are shape defects: a string coming back where a list was expected, stray whitespace, words getting split, or a crash on empty input. The parametrized sweep over widths, together with the range of input shapes, gives quick feedback on precisely those failure modes, and `pytest.mark.parametrize` makes adding new cases almost free. Snapshot-style expected outputs feel like the more rigorous option, but they largely just re-encode the implementation into the test — they verify that the code does what it does, not what it ought to do. My preference is to spend the assertion budget on properties every correct wrapper must satisfy, rather than on fixtures that need regenerating after each small change.

These tests intentionally verify the contract itself instead of hand-computing every expected literal. The parametrized reference-partition check makes sure the function matches the documented schema-walking semantics across a broad range of inputs, and the rest of the tests pin down the invariants that callers genuinely rely on: that the partition is complete and correctly ordered, what invalid entries look like, that valid records come through intact, and that inputs are never mutated. In my experience, suites full of hard-coded expected error strings turn into a maintenance burden with every small wording change or refactor — they break constantly, and reviewers end up approving them without really looking. Structural and property-style assertions are faster, more stable, and catch the regressions that actually happen in real code: dropped records, reordered indices, mutated inputs, or changed return shapes. The concrete test inputs still walk through the required, nullable, missing-field, and wrong-type branches, so decision-path coverage remains high without tying the suite to incidental details of the output.

The error handling here is intentionally lenient rather than strict. Deletion on this API is idempotent — asking to delete something that's already gone does nothing — so even if one request in the batch fails transiently, the overall run still converges toward the target state, and whatever is left over gets cleaned up by the next scheduled reconciliation pass. Killing the entire batch at the first sign of trouble would just strand a few hundred ids in a partially processed state, without buying us anything.

Since the caller owns the session and already has retry/backoff adapters and alerting on upstream failures, per-request status code checks would just re-implement machinery that exists elsewhere and clutter a loop that should stay conceptually simple. We log every response at debug level, which preserves an audit trail for post-mortems without polluting day-to-day output, and a warning on transport errors gives the operators watching the logs enough to act on. A timeout guards against a stuck connection stalling the whole batch. The net result: a readable happy path, a small function, and predictable behavior when things partially fail.

By design, the ingester takes a fail-soft approach at the line level. The log files it processes hold a blend of valid events and occasional partial writes — when a crash happens mid-flush, the last line ends up torn — and rejecting an entire batch over a single bad line would throw away all the good events that follow it. Because the job is scheduled and the log only ever grows via appends, anything skipped now is either permanently unparseable or gets picked up naturally once the writer finishes the line, so a hard failure buys us nothing.

Rather than tracking offsets line by line, the checkpoint moves to the end of whatever was read on each run. A single high-water mark stored in `meta` keeps the bookkeeping simple and correct even when truncation happens (we detect the file getting smaller and start over from zero), and it spares us a second write per event — which makes a real difference when a catch-up run chews through hundreds of thousands of lines. The insert loop and the checkpoint share the same connection and transaction, so the state written to SQLite is always internally consistent.

The summary handed back to the caller reports both lines read and events inserted, which is what the orchestrator's dashboards are driven by.
